Battle of El Alamein. The Battle of El Alamein was fought in October and November 1942 in the desert warfare near the village of El Alamein on Egypt's Mediterranean coast, sixty-six miles west of Alexandria. British General Bernard Montgomery halted German General Erwin Rommel's advance toward the Suez Canal and Cairo, inflicting his first major defeat. The victory allowed the British to counterattack and begin the liberation of North Africa, marking the Allies' first clear triumph over the Wehrmacht in sustained combat.

Erwin Rommel's Afrika Korps had pushed east across Libya and threatened Egypt, with British forces falling back to defend the Nile Delta. British General Bernard Montgomery assumed command of the Eighth Army in August 1942 and prepared a defensive stand at El Alamein.

The British established strong defensive positions with minefields, artillery, and anti-tank guns, avoiding the mobility warfare Rommel preferred. Fighting raged for eleven days from October 23 to November 4 with grinding, attritional combat. The British had numerical superiority in men and materiel. Rommel, outnumbered and short of fuel and ammunition, ordered a retreat. The Axis forces withdrew westward into Libya.

The British pursued Rommel westward while, combined with the American Operation Torch landings in Morocco and Algeria in November 1942, Axis forces were squeezed from both directions. El Alamein ended the myth of Rommel's invincibility in North Africa and restored British prestige after defeats at Tobruk and Gazala. The Allies secured control of the Mediterranean and prepared to invade Sicily and mainland Europe. Unlike Stalingrad's savage urban destruction, El Alamein was a textbook defensive victory and showcased Bernard Montgomery's methodical approach.
